questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes screening from diagnostic evaluation?
choices: Screening diagnoses every disease
Screening is generally for asymptomatic people; concerning symptoms require a diagnostic pathway
Diagnostic evaluation is never needed after screening
A normal screen excludes all future disease
questions.explanation: Screening identifies asymptomatic people who may need further evaluation. Symptoms such as bleeding, mass, weight loss, chest pain, or focal deficit require diagnostic assessment regardless of prior screening.

questions.question: Why should an FNP discuss potential harms of a screening test?
choices: Harms are irrelevant if the test is common
False positives, false negatives, downstream procedures, overdiagnosis, and access burden can affect patients
Only patients who decline screening need information
Screening tests never lead to additional testing
questions.explanation: Informed prevention includes meaningful discussion of possible benefits and harms. An abnormal screen often requires diagnostic testing, and a normal screen has limits.

questions.question: A patient has recent normal cancer screening but now reports persistent rectal bleeding and weight loss. What is the safest approach?
choices: Repeat routine screening only
Treat this as a diagnostic presentation and arrange appropriate evaluation
Reassure because screening was normal
Wait until the next screening interval
questions.explanation: New red-flag symptoms are not a screening issue. Prior normal screening does not explain or exclude a current concerning condition.

questions.question: What is an essential part of an immunization assessment?
choices: Rely only on memory of a static schedule
Assess status at encounters, reconcile records, check current guidance, and consider routine, catch-up, risk-based, and shared-decision recommendations
Avoid asking about prior doses
Assume a mild prior reaction is always a contraindication
questions.explanation: Immunization recommendations and products change. Verify records and current guidance, assess contraindications/precautions accurately, and document the plan.

questions.question: What does shared decision-making in preventive care require?
choices: The clinician makes the decision alone
Evidence, benefits/harms/alternatives/uncertainty, patient values, understanding, and a jointly chosen plan
A signature without discussion
Offering every test without prioritization
questions.explanation: Shared decisions integrate evidence with the individual patient’s values, goals, desired involvement, understanding, and practical ability to complete the plan.

questions.question: Why is the EHR preventive-care gap list not sufficient by itself?
choices: It is never useful
It is a prompt that still requires verification of records, current eligibility, risk, symptoms, and patient context
It replaces a history
It automatically determines contraindications
questions.explanation: EHR lists can be incomplete or outdated. The FNP verifies source records, current guidance, patient-specific risk, and whether a symptom changes the question from screening to diagnosis.

questions.question: Which action demonstrates closed-loop management of an abnormal screening result?
choices: Ordering a test without tracking it
Defining who contacts the patient, orders and tracks diagnostic completion, reviews results, and communicates next steps
Assuming the specialist will find the result
Telling the patient to call if concerned
questions.explanation: Abnormal screens require owned follow-up. Tracking completion and communicating results prevents avoidable diagnostic delay.

questions.question: What is the best way to approach a patient who declines a recommended preventive service?
choices: Shame the patient
Explore the reason respectfully, provide evidence-based information, document the decision, and invite future discussion
Remove the patient from care
Assume the reason is misinformation
questions.explanation: Respectful discussion identifies concerns, access barriers, and preferences. Patients can reconsider when they feel heard and have accurate information.

questions.question: Which is an example of quaternary prevention?
choices: Ordering every available test
Avoiding unnecessary tests or treatments that are unlikely to help and may cause harm
Ignoring abnormal findings
Delaying all preventive care
questions.explanation: Quaternary prevention protects patients from overtesting, overdiagnosis, unnecessary procedures, and treatment harm while preserving evidence-based care.

questions.question: What makes a preventive plan more likely to improve health?
choices: A long generic checklist
A prioritized, risk-based, access-aware plan with follow-up and patient-defined feasible steps
Only laboratory testing
Deferring all discussion until the next annual visit
questions.explanation: Plans work when they address the patient’s most important risks and goals, account for real barriers, specify next actions, and include follow-up and result ownership.
